title: CFEOM vs. Monocular Elevation Deficiency: A Masterclass in Congenital Motility Disorders
summary: Navigating the complexities of Congenital Cranial Dysinnervation Disorders (CCDDs) and isolated elevation deficits. This guide contrasts the genetic-driven restriction of CFEOM with the paretic/restrictive spectrum of Monocular Elevation Deficiency (Double Elevator Palsy).

sections.title: Clinical Definitions & Overview
sections.content: Congenital Fibrosis of the Extraocular Muscles (CFEOM) is a group of rare, non-progressive primary restrictive strabismus disorders characterized by the replacement of muscle tissue with fibrous tissue, now classified under Congenital Cranial Dysinnervation Disorders (CCDDs). Monocular Elevation Deficiency (MED), historically known as 'Double Elevator Palsy,' refers to a unilateral limitation of elevation in all positions of gaze, which can be paretic, restrictive, or supranuclear in origin.

rows: Dysgenesis of the oculomotor (CN III) or trochlear (CN IV) nuclei/nerves leading to secondary muscle fibrosis.
Heterogeneous: Can be restrictive (IR fibrosis), paretic (SR/IO weakness), or supranuclear (pretectal lesion).
Typically sporadic; rarely associated with syndromes.
Abnormal 'misfiring' or absence of cranial nerve subnuclei.
Deficient neural drive to the Superior Rectus and Inferior Oblique.

branches: CFEOM 1: KIF21A mutation, AD, classic phenotype, bilateral.
CFEOM 2: PHOX2A mutation, AR, ptosis, exotropic/fixed gaze.
CFEOM 3: TUBB3 mutation, AD, variable severity, can be unilateral.
Tukel Syndrome: CFEOM features + postaxial oligodactyly.

sections.title: Hallmark Clinical Features
content: CFEOM: Severe ptosis (bilateral), eyes fixed in infraduction (usually <10 degrees above midline).
CFEOM: Compensatory chin-up head position to maintain fusion or see.
MED: Unilateral elevation deficit in abduction, adduction, and primary gaze.
MED: Marcus Gunn Jaw-winking (found in ~25% of cases).
MED: True ptosis or Pseudoptosis (due to hypotropic eye).

sections.title: Mandatory Diagnostic Workup
content: Step 1: Forced Duction Test (FDT) - Essential to differentiate restriction (positive) from palsy (negative).
Step 2: Force Generation Test (FGT) - Assesses active muscle strength.
Step 3: Saccadic Velocity - Slowed up-saccades suggest paresis; abrupt stop suggests restriction.
Step 4: Bell's Phenomenon - Absent in CFEOM and Type 1/2 MED; preserved in supranuclear MED.
Step 5: High-Resolution MRI - Visualize CN III, IV, and VI; look for muscle atrophy/hypoplasia.

rows: Restriction ONLY in adduction; V-pattern divergence in upgaze.
Acquired, proptosis, eyelid retraction, lid lag.
History of trauma, diplopia, infraorbital anesthesia.

sections.title: Surgical Management: CFEOM
content: Goal: Move eyes to primary position and address head tilt.
Large Recessions: Bilateral Inferior Rectus recessions (often 8-12mm or more).
Adjuncts: Use of hang-back sutures or adjustable sutures.
Ptosis: Frontalis suspension is standard. Caution: Risk of exposure keratopathy due to poor Bell's phenomenon.

sections.title: Surgical Management: MED
content: Step 1: Perform FDT in OR. If positive IR restriction -> Recess Inferior Rectus.
Step 2: If FDT is negative (Paretic Type) -> Knapp Procedure.
Step 3: Knapp Procedure involves transposing MR and LR to the insertion of the SR.
Step 4: Address Ptosis ONLY after the hypotropia is corrected (to avoid worsening pseudoptosis).

sections.title: CRITICAL RED FLAGS
content: Exposure Keratopathy: Post-ptosis surgery risk is extremely high in CFEOM due to absent Bell's and restricted downgaze.
Malignant Hyperthermia: Increased risk in some congenital myopathies/fibrosis syndromes.
Corneal Anesthesia: Associated with CFEOM2 (PHOX2A) due to CN V involvement.
Amblyopia: Rapid development in unilateral MED or CFEOM3; requires aggressive patching.

content.explanation: P: Paretic (SR/IO palsy), R: Restrictive (IR fibrosis), S: Supranuclear (Pretectal).

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Exam Prep
content: Knapp Procedure: Full tendon transposition of MR and LR to SR insertion. Expect ~20-30 PD correction.
Pseudo-ptosis: In MED, the upper lid follows the hypotropic eye down. Occlude the 'good' eye; if the lid lifts as the eye takes up fixation, it is pseudoptosis.
CFEOM1: Always bilateral, symmetrical, and involves the Superior Division of CN III.
In CFEOM, horizontal deviations (Exotropia/Esotropia) are common and should be corrected simultaneously with vertical deviations.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Research
sections.content: The 'CCDD' paradigm shift has moved our understanding from primary muscle pathology to primary neurogenic dysgenesis. Recent studies using 3T and 7T MRI have confirmed the absence of the abducens or oculomotor nerves in specific CFEOM phenotypes. Landmark studies by Elizabeth Engle have mapped the genetic loci (KIF21A), proving that these disorders result from kinesin motor protein defects affecting axonal guidance.
